title: Why Thrifted Outdoor Gear Makes Sense for Nairobi Hikers
meta_title: Thrifted Outdoor Gear in Nairobi: 6 Solid Buys, 3 to Skip
meta_description: Thrifted outdoor gear in Nairobi: which jackets, boots and packs are worth buying pre-owned, what to buy new and how to check each piece before you pay.
excerpt: Thrifted outdoor gear in Nairobi can give you branded jackets, boots and packs for less. Here is what to buy pre-owned, what to buy new and how to check every piece.
content:
A waterproof shell built for Scottish rain or Alpine snow often ends up on a rail in Kenya with years of life left, which is why thrifted outdoor gear in Nairobi is such good value. Buy pre-owned jackets, fleeces, down, rucksacks and boots with healthy soles; buy socks, underwear and any climbing safety kit new.

The catch is that every used piece has its own history. A jacket can look perfect and still leak at the seams, and a barely worn boot can hide a crumbling midsole. Below: which items repay a second-hand purchase, how to check each one in minutes, how to care for it, and where to shop.

Quick Facts

  • Best thrifted buys: shells, fleeces, down jackets, rucksacks and boots with healthy soles.
  • Buy new: socks, underwear, gas cartridges and climbing safety kit.
  • Hidden faults: peeling jacket membranes and crumbling boot midsoles.
  • Jacket test: water flicked on the shoulders should bead, not soak in.
  • Rainy seasons: long rains roughly March-May, short rains roughly October-December.
  • Where to buy thrifted outdoor gear in Nairobi: Mountain Mall, 3rd Floor, Shop D39, Thika Road, or online.

What Counts as Thrifted Outdoor Gear in Nairobi?

Thrifted outdoor gear in Nairobi means pre-owned hiking and camping kit, mostly from European and American brands, resold here after a first owner abroad. It sits alongside new stock in many shops, so you can mix the two.

The North Face, Columbia, Regatta, Berghaus and Karrimor turn up regularly in Kenya's second-hand trade. Technical clothing is built to survive storms, scree and rucksack straps, so a jacket that saw a few winter weekends in Europe often has most of its working life left. You pay for that remaining life, not for a new label.

The trade-off is choice: thrifted pieces are one-offs, so your exact size may not be on the rail this week. Most Nairobi hikers end up with a mixed kit of a pre-owned shell and fleece, new socks, and boots chosen on fit. Our hiking gear checklist for Kenya and beginner hiking gear guide show how those pieces fit together.

Which Items Are Worth Buying Pre-Owned, and Which Should Be New?

When you shop for thrifted outdoor gear in Nairobi, outer layers, insulation and packs are the safest buys because their faults are visible. Anything worn against skin, anything pressurised and anything that holds your body weight on a rope is better bought new.

The UIAA (the international mountaineering federation) advises against second-hand harnesses, helmets and ropes because their integrity cannot be confirmed. Few Kenyan hikes need them; if yours does, buy new.

Waterproof jackets and rain pants

A used shell is the best-value piece of thrifted outdoor gear in Nairobi, and the short rains make it a timely one. Look for a named membrane such as Gore-Tex, or a waterproof rating on the care label. Pair it with waterproof rain pants if you hike the Aberdares or Mt Kenya's forest zone, where afternoon storms soak trousers in minutes. The rain jackets section of our shop lists the shells currently available.

Fleeces and down jackets

Fleece is the lowest-risk thrifted outdoor gear in Nairobi because it is almost impossible to ruin. Down needs a closer look: squeeze a baffle and it should spring back within seconds. Flat, clumped sections usually mean damp storage or the wrong detergent.

Boots and rucksacks

Boots are where thrifted outdoor gear in Nairobi needs the closest look: uppers age slowly, but the sole unit tells you what you are really buying. Our post on judging second hand hiking boots walks through the sole checks in detail. With packs, load a few kilos and wear it; collapsed hip-belt foam pushes weight onto your shoulders.

How Do You Check Used Hiking Gear Before Paying?

Give every piece of thrifted outdoor gear in Nairobi a careful five-minute look in good light before you pay. Turn it inside out, work every zip and buckle, and try it on with the layers you will actually wear on the trail.

  1. Turn jackets inside out and check the seam tape at the shoulders and hood. Lifting tape or a flaking inner lining means leaks.
  2. Flick water on the shoulders. Beading means the water-repellent finish works; wet patches mean it needs re-proofing, which is fixable.
  3. Run every zip end to end. A sticky zip can be cleaned; missing teeth usually cannot.
  4. Flex boot soles and look for midsole cracks and gaps along the glue line.
  5. Press a thumbnail into the midsole. Springy is good; chalky crumbling signals hydrolysis.
  6. Load-test rucksack buckles, hip-belt foam and strap stitching.
  7. Sniff down and boot linings. Mildew is hard to remove.

Boot makers such as Meindl explain that polyurethane midsoles break down when boots sit unused, especially in damp storage, so an unworn-looking pair can be the riskiest buy. Even tread wear from regular use is often the safer sign.

Fit matters more than condition. A perfect boot half a size too small will cost you toenails on the descent from Mt Longonot's crater rim, so try boots in the afternoon, wearing your hiking socks.

How Should You Clean and Care for Pre-Owned Outdoor Gear?

Thrifted outdoor gear in Nairobi has already had at least one owner, so wash each piece once when you bring it home, then follow the care label. Correct washing restores water repellency on shells and loft in down.

For waterproof shells, Gore-Tex's own care instructions say to close every zip, wash at 40°C with a little liquid detergent, rinse twice and avoid powder, fabric softener and bleach. A further 20 minutes in a warm tumble dryer reactivates the water-repellent finish; with no dryer, use a low iron with a cloth over the fabric. If water still soaks in, apply a pump-spray or wash-in re-proofer.

Boots need regular wear more than anything. Brush off mud after each hike, dry them slowly at room temperature with the tongues open, never beside a jiko, and store them somewhere dry and airy. Wash down only with a down-specific wash, and store it loose rather than compressed.

Pro Tips for Thrifting Hiking Gear

  • Shop for thrifted outdoor gear in Nairobi in September or February, before the short or long rains start.
  • Bring the base layer and fleece you hike in when trying on a shell, so you size for layers.
  • Prefer boots with honest tread wear over pristine pairs that may have spent years in storage.
  • Buy socks new and spend the savings on better boots.

Is Second-Hand Kit Good Enough for Mt Kenya or Kilimanjaro?

Yes, for most of the kit list. Thrifted outdoor gear in Nairobi can take you to Point Lenana at 4,985 m or Uhuru Peak at 5,895 m if each piece passes the checks above. The exceptions are socks, underwear and any warm layer that fails the loft test.

Summit night, well below freezing before dawn, is where weak gear shows, so your down jacket and gloves matter most. Our list of Mt Kenya gear to buy in Nairobi covers every layer, and the Kilimanjaro gear guide adds what changes on the longer climb.

Day hikes such as Ngong Hills or the Longonot crater need far less: decent boots, a rain shell, a warm layer and a small pack.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is thrifted outdoor gear in Nairobi actually good quality?

Thrifted outdoor gear in Nairobi is often very good quality because much of it comes from established brands built for harsher weather than Kenya's day hikes. Quality varies piece by piece, though, so judge each item on its own condition: seam tape, zips, membranes, loft in down and the state of boot soles. A well-kept pre-owned shell will outperform a cheap new one.

Can a second hand rain jacket still be waterproof?

A second hand rain jacket can be fully waterproof if its membrane and seam tape are intact. Surface water soaking into the outer fabric usually means only the water-repellent finish has worn off, which a wash and re-proofing restores. Flaking inner coating or lifting seam tape cannot be fixed easily, so leave that jacket on the rail.

How do I know if used hiking boots will fall apart?

Used hiking boots are most likely to fall apart when the polyurethane midsole has hydrolysed after long storage. Flex the sole and look for fine cracks, press the midsole to check it is springy rather than chalky, and examine the glue line between sole and upper. Even tread wear from regular use is a reassuring sign.

Final Thoughts

Second-hand kit rewards a careful eye far more than luck. Shells, fleeces, down and packs are where pre-owned buying pays off; socks, gas and climbing safety kit belong on the new list; and boots are worth buying used only when the sole passes a close look.
